expected_evidence: geological: platinum/iridium anomaly, magnetic spherules, meltglass, nanodiamonds at the Younger Dryas boundary layer (e.g., Abu Hureyra, Syria — the actual site cited in the real-world Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis literature, Bunch et al. 2020)
material/archaeological: occupation hiatus, abrupt settlement abandonment or reorganization layer, destruction/burn horizon at Epipaleolithic-to-early-Neolithic transition sites in the Levant

genetic/bioarchaeological: skeletal evidence of trauma or mass mortality, population bottleneck or discontinuity signal in the Natufian-to-PPNA demographic sequence (ancient DNA at this time depth is rarely preserved in the region)

astronomical: modeled airburst mechanics/trajectory reconstructions, correlation with broader Younger Dryas boundary event markers across multiple continents (no impact crater expected for an airburst)
oral_tradition: possible deluge/catastrophe myth motifs retrojected onto this period, but any transmission chain over ~13,000 years is extremely weak and speculative

iconographic: contested symbolic imagery (e.g., Göbekli Tepe Pillar 43 'Vulture Stone' interpretations by Sweatman & Tsikritsis) claimed to encode the event — highly disputed, model-prior-level association only
response.rationale: This hypothesis matches the real, contested Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis as applied to the Middle East (Abu Hureyra, Syria), placing an airburst-linked demographic corroboration at ~10,850 BCE — inside the younger-dryas period window (~10,900–9,700 BCE) rather than a clearly specified period label, so I am scoring it against the younger-dryas row since the interval falls there. Geological evidence (platinum spikes, meltglass, nanodiamonds) has the highest detectability (0.65) in this table and is indeed the category most frequently cited by proponents (Bunch et al. 2020), though its interpretation remains disputed by other geologists (Holliday, Boslough, Daulton), so absence-of-consensus here reflects contested interpretation rather than pure non-detectability. Astronomical detectability is listed unusually high (0.7), but for a Pleistocene/early-Holocene airburst this mostly means indirect multi-site correlative modeling rather than direct observational astronomy — I would not weight this as strongly as the table implies for a 'population-demography' object. The hypothesis's core claim (demographic impact) is best evidenced by genetic/skeletal and material-archaeological data, both of which sit at low-to-moderate detectability (0.3 and 0.35) due to poor preservation, small sample sizes, and general scarcity of skeletal populations from this era — a low-evidence outcome here is expected and should not be read as falsifying the hypothesis. Textual, linguistic, oral_tradition, and iconographic evidence are all near-zero to low (0.0–0.1), consistent with this being long before writing and with iconographic claims (e.g., Göbekli Tepe) remaining speculative model-prior-level associations rather than established fact. Given this mix — one moderately-plausible geological channel, weak-to-moderate material/genetic channels, and near-zero symbolic/textual channels — I suggest an aggregate detectability_adjustment of ~0.4, meaning limited or contested surviving evidence is the expected default outcome for this hypothesis, and should temper strong claims of either confirmation or refutation.
